stem:
The stereoisomer of 1-chloro-2,6-dimethylcyclohexane drawn here undergoes {{E2}} elimination with {{NaOCH3}} far more slowly than any of its other stereoisomers. Explain why.
[[ring:1u:Cl,2d:CH3,6d:CH3]]
model:
{{E2}} needs the hydrogen and the leaving group anti-periplanar. On a cyclohexane that means trans-diaxial: an axial Cl with an axial H on the carbon next to it.

In this isomer Cl is trans to both methyl groups. In the stable chair all three groups are equatorial. Cl is equatorial, so no hydrogen is anti to it.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH3,6d:CH3|B]]

Flipping the ring makes Cl axial, but both methyl groups become axial too. They fill the axial positions on C2 and C6, so the hydrogens on those carbons are equatorial. There is still no H anti to Cl, and this chair is strained and rare as well.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH3,6d:CH3|A]]

In the other stereoisomers at least one methyl is cis to Cl. With Cl axial, a cis methyl is equatorial, so its carbon has an axial hydrogen anti to Cl, and {{E2}} is fast. For example, the all-cis isomer:

[[chair:1u:Cl,2u:CH3,6u:CH3|A]]

rubric.h: States the requirement: H and Cl anti-periplanar, which on a cyclohexane means trans-diaxial on neighbouring carbons
Stable chair: Cl equatorial, so no hydrogen is anti to it
Flipped chair: Cl axial, but both methyls axial, so the hydrogens on C2 and C6 are equatorial (still no anti H)
Other isomers have a methyl cis to Cl, which gives an axial H next to an axial Cl

steps.h: Anti-periplanar H and leaving group. On a ring: both axial, on neighbouring carbons.

ask.q: Which carbons could supply the hydrogen here?
ask.a: C2 and C6, the two carbons next to the C-Cl carbon. Each has one H and one {{CH3}}.

steps.h: Cl is up. Both methyls are down. Cl is trans to each of its neighbours' methyl groups, so it is cis to each of their hydrogens.
Trans neighbours are both equatorial or both axial. In one chair all three groups are equatorial. Equatorial Cl: nothing can happen.

ask.q: What is anti to an equatorial Cl?
ask.a: A C-C bond of the ring, not a hydrogen.

steps.h: Now all three groups are axial. Cl is in position, but the axial places on C2 and C6 hold methyl groups. Their hydrogens are equatorial.

ask.q: Does this chair have an H anti to Cl?
ask.a: No. And with three axial groups it is rare anyway.

steps.h: A methyl that is cis to Cl is equatorial when Cl is axial, which leaves an axial H on that carbon. Both other isomers have at least one such methyl, so they have a reactive chair.

solution.answer: Neither chair has an axial Cl next to an axial H: in one Cl is equatorial, in the other the axial positions next to Cl hold methyl groups. The other isomers have a chair with Cl and a neighbouring H both axial.
solution.rule: If every neighbour's substituent is trans to the leaving group, no hydrogen can ever be anti to it.

stem:
cis-1-Bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane undergoes {{E2}} elimination with base several hundred times faster than the trans isomer. Both give 4-tert-butylcyclohexene. Explain the difference in rate.
[[ring:1u:Br,4u:C(CH3)3]]
[[ring:1d:Br,4u:C(CH3)3]]
model:
{{E2}} needs H and Br anti-periplanar: on a cyclohexane, Br axial with an axial H on the next carbon (trans-diaxial).

The tert-butyl group is so large (5.5 kcal/mol, K = 11,916) that it is equatorial in essentially every molecule. That fixes the position of Br.

Cis isomer: with tert-butyl equatorial, Br is axial. The axial hydrogens on C2 and C6 are anti to it. Every molecule is ready to react: fast.

[[chair:1u:Br,4u:C(CH3)3|A]]

Trans isomer: with tert-butyl equatorial, Br is equatorial. No hydrogen is anti to an equatorial Br, so this chair cannot react.

[[chair:1d:Br,4u:C(CH3)3|A]]

The trans isomer can react only from the flipped chair, where Br is axial but tert-butyl is axial too. Only about 1 molecule in 12,000 is in that chair at any moment, so the reaction is slow.

[[chair:1d:Br,4u:C(CH3)3|B]]

rubric.h: States the requirement: anti-periplanar, trans-diaxial H and Br
tert-Butyl stays equatorial (locks the ring), with the A-value or K as support
Cis: Br axial in the locked chair, with axial H on the neighbouring carbons, so it reacts fast
Trans: Br equatorial in the locked chair, no anti H; it must react through the rare chair with tert-butyl axial, so it is slow

steps.h: Br axial, H axial on the neighbouring carbon.
From the lecture table, tert-butyl costs 5.5 kcal/mol when axial: K = 11,916. It stays equatorial.

ask.a: No, it still flips, but the chair with tert-butyl axial is almost empty: about 1 molecule in 12,000.

steps.t: Place Br in the cis isomer
steps.h: A cis-1,4 pair is one axial, one equatorial. tert-Butyl takes equatorial, so Br is axial.

ask.q: Which hydrogens are anti to it?
ask.a: The axial hydrogens on C2 and C6.

steps.t: Place Br in the trans isomer
steps.h: A trans-1,4 pair is both equatorial or both axial. With tert-butyl equatorial, Br is equatorial: no anti hydrogen.

steps.t: Say how the trans isomer reacts at all
steps.h: Through the flipped chair with both groups axial. Its tiny population is the reason for the low rate.

ask.q: Why do both isomers give the same alkene?
ask.a: The C-Br carbon stops being a stereocentre when it becomes part of the C=C.

solution.answer: tert-Butyl locks the ring. Cis: Br is held axial, anti to axial H on both sides, fast. Trans: Br is held equatorial with no anti H, and must react through the rare chair with tert-butyl axial, slow.
solution.rule: Leaving group cis to a 4-tert-butyl: axial, fast E2. Trans: equatorial, slow E2.

stem:
Neomenthyl chloride reacts with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in ethanol about 200 times faster than menthyl chloride. Neomenthyl chloride gives mainly the alkene with the double bond toward the isopropyl group. Menthyl chloride gives only the alkene with the double bond away from it. Explain both observations.

Neomenthyl chloride: [[ring:1d:Cl,2d:CH(CH3)2,5u:CH3]]
Menthyl chloride: [[ring:1u:Cl,2d:CH(CH3)2,5u:CH3]]
model:
{{E2}} needs H and Cl anti-periplanar: Cl axial with an axial H on a neighbouring carbon.

Neomenthyl chloride. In the stable chair isopropyl and methyl are equatorial and Cl is axial. C2 (with the equatorial isopropyl) and C6 both have an axial H anti to Cl. The stable chair reacts, so the reaction is fast, and with two hydrogens to choose from the more substituted alkene (Saytzeff, double bond toward the isopropyl carbon) is major.

[[chair:1d:Cl,2d:CH(CH3)2,5u:CH3|B]]

Menthyl chloride. In the stable chair all three groups are equatorial, including Cl: no anti H, no reaction from this chair.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH(CH3)2,5u:CH3|B]]

It must flip to the chair with all three groups axial, which is strained and rare: slow. In that chair the isopropyl group, trans to Cl, takes the axial place on C2, so the H on C2 is equatorial. Only C6 has an axial H. The double bond can form only away from the isopropyl group, although that alkene is less substituted.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH(CH3)2,5u:CH3|A]]

rubric.h: States the requirement: trans-diaxial H and Cl
Neomenthyl: Cl axial in the stable chair, axial H on both neighbours: fast, and Saytzeff alkene major
Menthyl: Cl equatorial in the stable chair; reacts only through the all-axial chair: slow
Menthyl, product: in the reacting chair the H on the isopropyl carbon is equatorial, so only the other neighbour can lose H

steps.h: Axial Cl, axial H next door.
The two large groups, isopropyl (2.61 kcal/mol) and methyl (1.74), can both be equatorial in one chair. In that chair Cl is axial in neomenthyl chloride and equatorial in menthyl chloride.

ask.q: The two compounds differ at one carbon. Which?
ask.a: C1, the carbon with Cl. Its Cl is cis to the isopropyl in neomenthyl and trans in menthyl.

steps.h: Cl is already axial in the chair nearly every molecule adopts. Fast.
Isopropyl is equatorial, so C2 has an axial H. C6 has one too. Two choices: Saytzeff picks the double bond toward the isopropyl carbon.

ask.q: Why is that alkene more substituted?
ask.a: The isopropyl group sits on the C=C: three carbons on the double bond instead of two.

steps.h: Cl is equatorial in the stable chair. The ring must flip to put Cl axial, which makes isopropyl and methyl axial as well: costly, so few molecules are in it.
In the flipped chair the axial place on C2 holds the isopropyl. The H on C2 is equatorial and cannot leave. Only the axial H on C6 can: double bond away from the isopropyl.

ask.q: Does the Saytzeff rule fail here?
ask.a: It does not apply: only one hydrogen is anti, so there is no choice to make.

solution.answer: Neomenthyl: Cl axial in the stable chair with two anti hydrogens, fast, Saytzeff alkene. Menthyl: must use the rare all-axial chair, slow, and there only C6 has an anti hydrogen, so only the less substituted alkene forms.
solution.rule: The rate depends on how common the reactive chair is. The product depends on which hydrogens are axial in it.

stem:
Bromocyclohexane has two chairs, one with Br axial and one with Br equatorial. Explain why the {{E2}} reaction with a base can take place only from the chair with Br axial.
[[chair:1u:Br|A]]
[[chair:1u:Br|B]]
model:
{{E2}} needs the leaving group and the hydrogen anti-periplanar: on neighbouring carbons, in the same plane, pointing in opposite directions. Then the C-H electrons can push in from behind the C-Br bond, the overlap is best and the transition state is the most stable.

Br axial. The axial bonds on neighbouring carbons point in opposite directions. The axial H on C2 (and the one on C6) is exactly anti to the axial Br. The reaction can go.

Br equatorial. Look along the C1-C2 bond. Anti to the equatorial Br is the ring bond from C2 to C3, not a hydrogen. Both hydrogens on C2 are gauche to Br (about 60°). The same is true on C6. No hydrogen is anti, so this chair cannot react.

rubric.h: States the anti-periplanar requirement (and that it gives the best overlap or most stable transition state)
Axial Br: the axial H on the next carbon is anti to it
Equatorial Br: anti to it is a ring C-C bond; both neighbouring hydrogens are gauche

steps.h: Anti-periplanar H and leaving group. The lecture: the electrons back-attack, like {{SN2}}.
Axial bonds alternate up and down, so an axial Br on C1 and an axial H on C2 point opposite ways and lie in one plane with the C1-C2 bond: anti.
The lecture's Newman projection of methylcyclohexane shows an equatorial group anti to a ring carbon. The same holds for Br: what is anti to it is the C2-C3 bond. The hydrogens are at 60°.

solution.answer: Only an axial Br has an axial H anti to it on the next carbon. Anti to an equatorial Br is a ring C-C bond, so no hydrogen can be removed.
solution.rule: Equatorial leaving group: anti to a ring bond, no E2.

stem:
Bromocyclohexane slightly prefers the chair with Br equatorial, and an equatorial Br cannot undergo {{E2}}. Yet bromocyclohexane reacts readily with {{NaOCH2CH3}} to give cyclohexene. Explain.
[[ring:1u:Br]]
model:
{{E2}} needs Br axial, with an axial H on the next carbon (anti-periplanar, trans-diaxial).

The two chairs of bromocyclohexane interconvert rapidly by the ring flip, and they differ very little in energy: Br is a small group (about 0.5 kcal/mol, against 1.74 for methyl and 5.5 for tert-butyl). So a large share of the molecules have Br axial at any moment.

[[chair:1u:Br|B]] [[chair:1u:Br|A]]

The molecules with Br axial react, through the axial H on C2 or C6. As they are used up, the ring flip keeps supplying more. The reaction is not held back.

Only when another group makes the axial-Br chair very unfavourable (for example a tert-butyl group that would have to be axial) does the reaction become slow.

rubric.h: Requirement: Br must be axial with an axial H on the neighbouring carbon
The two chairs interconvert and are close in energy, so many molecules have Br axial
Reaction goes through the axial chair, and the flip replaces the molecules that react

steps.h: Axial Br, axial H next door.
Nothing but the small Br changes position. The cost of axial Br is small, so the axial chair is well populated.
The rate depends on how many molecules are in the reactive chair. Here that is a large fraction, and the fast ring flip keeps refilling it.

solution.answer: The chair with Br axial is only slightly less stable and forms constantly by the ring flip, so plenty of molecules are in the reactive chair.
solution.rule: A less stable chair still reacts if it is easy to reach.

stem:
With {{NaOCH3}} in {{CH3OH}}, cis-1-chloro-2-methylcyclohexane undergoes {{E2}} faster than the trans isomer, and the two isomers give different major alkenes: 1-methylcyclohexene from cis, 3-methylcyclohexene from trans. Explain both facts.

cis: [[ring:1u:Cl,2u:CH3]] trans: [[ring:1u:Cl,2d:CH3]]
model:
{{E2}} needs H and Cl trans-diaxial (anti-periplanar).

Cis isomer. In the chair with Cl axial, the methyl is equatorial. This is the more stable chair, so most molecules are ready to react. C2 has an axial H (anti to Cl) and so does C6. With both available, the more substituted alkene forms: 1-methylcyclohexene (Saytzeff).

[[chair:1u:Cl,2u:CH3|A]]

Trans isomer. The stable chair has both groups equatorial and cannot react. In the chair with Cl axial the methyl is axial too: this chair is less stable (an axial methyl costs 1.74 kcal/mol, and Cl is axial as well), so fewer molecules are in it and the reaction is slower.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:CH3|A]]

In that chair the axial place on C2 holds the methyl, so the H on C2 is equatorial and cannot leave. Only C6 has an axial H: the double bond forms away from the methyl, giving 3-methylcyclohexene.

rubric.h: Requirement: trans-diaxial H and Cl
Cis: Cl axial with methyl equatorial (stable chair); axial H on C2 and C6; Saytzeff gives 1-methylcyclohexene
Trans: reacting chair has Cl and methyl both axial, less populated, so slower
Trans: H on C2 is equatorial in that chair, so only C6 can lose H: 3-methylcyclohexene

steps.h: Cl axial, H axial on a neighbouring carbon.

steps.t: Draw each isomer with Cl axial
steps.h: Cis: methyl equatorial. Trans: methyl axial.
For cis the reactive chair is the stable one. For trans it is the unstable diaxial one, so only a small fraction of the molecules can react at any moment.
Cis: axial H on C2 and C6, so Saytzeff applies. Trans: the methyl occupies the axial place on C2, so only C6 has an axial H.

solution.answer: Cis reacts from its stable chair and has an axial H on the methyl carbon: fast, 1-methylcyclohexene. Trans must use the diaxial chair, where only C6 has an axial H: slower, 3-methylcyclohexene.
solution.rule: The same chair analysis explains the rate and the product.

stem:
The all-trans isomer of 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane undergoes {{E2}} 7000 times more slowly than any other stereoisomer. The isomer drawn here differs from it at one carbon only (C1). Explain why this small change makes {{E2}} fast, and say which H and which Cl leave.
[[ring:1d:Cl,2d:Cl,3u:Cl,4d:Cl,5u:Cl,6d:Cl|num]]
model:
{{E2}} needs a Cl and an H trans-diaxial on neighbouring carbons.

In the all-trans isomer every Cl is equatorial in one chair, and every H is equatorial in the other: an axial Cl never sits next to an axial H.

In this isomer the Cl on C1 is on the same face as the Cl atoms on C2 and C6. In the chair that keeps the other five Cl equatorial, the Cl on C1 is axial.

[[chair:1d:Cl,2d:Cl,3u:Cl,4d:Cl,5u:Cl,6d:Cl|B]]

C2 and C6 have their Cl equatorial, so their hydrogens are axial, pointing to the opposite face from the Cl on C1: anti-periplanar. The base removes the axial H from C2 (or C6) while the axial Cl on C1 leaves. This chair has only one axial Cl, so it is the stable chair and the reaction is fast.

rubric.h: Requirement: trans-diaxial Cl and H on neighbouring carbons
In the chair with five Cl equatorial, the Cl on C1 is axial
The H on C2 and on C6 is axial and anti to that Cl (because their Cl is equatorial, cis to the Cl on C1)
Names what leaves: the Cl on C1 and the H on C2 or C6; this is the stable chair, so it is fast

steps.h: An axial Cl next to an axial H.
In the all-trans isomer the faces alternate all the way round. Here C1, C2 and C6 all have Cl down: the Cl on C1 is cis to both neighbours.
Five Cl can be equatorial together. The sixth, on C1, has to be axial.
A neighbour whose Cl is cis to the axial Cl has that Cl equatorial and its H axial. So C2 and C6 each offer an anti hydrogen.

solution.answer: The Cl on C1 is axial in the stable chair, and the hydrogens on C2 and C6 are axial and anti to it. The Cl on C1 and the H on C2 (or C6) leave.
solution.rule: One pair of cis neighbouring Cl atoms is enough to give an axial Cl next to an axial H.

stem:
trans-1-Bromo-4-tert-butylcyclohexane undergoes {{E2}} very slowly. trans-1-Bromo-4-methylcyclohexane, which has the same shape with a smaller group, reacts far faster. Explain, using the lecture's values for methyl and tert-butyl.
[[ring:1d:Br,4u:CH3]]
[[ring:1d:Br,4u:C(CH3)3]]
model:
{{E2}} needs Br axial with an axial H on the next carbon.

In both compounds the groups are trans-1,4, so they are both equatorial in one chair and both axial in the other. Only the diaxial chair has Br axial, so both compounds must react through it.

[[chair:1d:Br,4u:CH3|A]] [[chair:1d:Br,4u:CH3|B]]

The difference is how many molecules are in that chair. An axial methyl costs 1.74 kcal/mol (K = 19.5): roughly 1 molecule in 20 has the methyl axial, so the reactive chair is easy to reach. An axial tert-butyl costs 5.5 kcal/mol (K = 11,916): roughly 1 molecule in 12,000. The tert-butyl compound has hundreds of times fewer molecules able to react, so it is far slower.

rubric.h: Requirement: Br axial, anti to an axial H
Both trans isomers have Br axial only in the diaxial chair
Methyl: 1.74 kcal/mol, K = 19.5, so the diaxial chair is reasonably populated
tert-Butyl: 5.5 kcal/mol, K = 11,916, so the diaxial chair is almost empty and the reaction is slow

steps.h: Br axial.
Trans-1,4: both equatorial or both axial. The reactive chair is the one with both axial, for both compounds.
Putting methyl axial: K = 19.5. Putting tert-butyl axial: K = 11,916. (Br itself costs little, and the same in both.)
The fraction of molecules in the reactive chair is about 600 times smaller for the tert-butyl compound (11,916 / 19.5), so its E2 is far slower.

solution.answer: Both must react through the diaxial chair. With methyl that chair holds about 1 molecule in 20; with tert-butyl about 1 in 12,000. Fewer reactive molecules, slower E2.
solution.rule: The bigger the group that must go axial, the slower the E2.

stem:
A classmate explains the slow {{E2}} of the all-trans hexachlorocyclohexane this way: "All the Cl are equatorial, so the molecule just has to flip its ring. Then every Cl is axial and elimination is easy. It is slow only because the flipped chair is crowded." What is right and what is wrong in this answer? Write the correct explanation.
[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:Cl,3u:Cl,4d:Cl,5u:Cl,6d:Cl|B]]
model:
Right: {{E2}} needs an axial Cl, the drawn chair has none, and the flipped chair with six axial Cl is crowded and rare.

Wrong: elimination is not easy from the flipped chair either. {{E2}} needs an axial Cl and an axial H on the next carbon. The ring flip changes every position at once: when all six Cl become axial, all six H become equatorial.

[[chair:1u:Cl,2d:Cl,3u:Cl,4d:Cl,5u:Cl,6d:Cl|A]]

So in the flipped chair each axial Cl has only equatorial hydrogens next to it, and none of them is anti-periplanar. The reason is the stereochemistry, which no flip can change: each Cl is trans to the Cl on both neighbouring carbons, so it is cis to both neighbouring hydrogens. A cis H and Cl are never both axial.

Correct explanation: neither chair has an axial Cl next to an axial H, so the anti-periplanar geometry cannot be reached in a chair at all. Every other stereoisomer has at least one Cl cis to a neighbouring Cl, which gives a chair with an axial Cl next to an axial H.

rubric.h: Credits what is right: an axial Cl is needed, and the all-axial chair is strained
Identifies the error: after the flip every H is equatorial, so there is still no H anti to any Cl
Gives the stereochemical reason: each Cl is trans to its neighbours' Cl, so cis to their H
States that other isomers have a chair with axial Cl next to axial H

steps.h: Not just an axial Cl: an axial Cl and an axial H on the neighbouring carbon.
On each carbon the Cl and the H swap roles. Six equatorial Cl and six axial H become six axial Cl and six equatorial H.
In the first chair: axial H, but equatorial Cl. In the second: axial Cl, but equatorial H. Neither chair has both.
Cis and trans are fixed. An H and a Cl on neighbouring carbons can be trans-diaxial only if they are trans. Here every such pair is cis.

solution.answer: The classmate is right that an axial Cl is needed and that the flipped chair is strained, but wrong that it can react: after the flip every H is equatorial. No chair has an axial Cl next to an axial H.
solution.rule: The ring flip swaps axial and equatorial on every carbon. It never turns a cis pair into a trans pair.

stem:
Three stereoisomers of 1-bromo-2-methyl-4-tert-butylcyclohexane are treated with {{NaOCH2CH3}} in ethanol. Isomers X and Y react quickly. Isomer Z reacts far more slowly. (a) Explain why Z is slow. (b) X and Y give different major alkenes. Explain which way the double bond forms in each.

X: [[ring:1u:Br,2u:CH3,4u:C(CH3)3]]
Y: [[ring:1u:Br,2d:CH3,4u:C(CH3)3]]
Z: [[ring:1d:Br,2u:CH3,4u:C(CH3)3]]
model:
{{E2}} needs Br axial and an axial H on a neighbouring carbon. The tert-butyl group stays equatorial (5.5 kcal/mol, K = 11,916), so each isomer has one chair that matters.

(a) Z. With tert-butyl equatorial, Br (trans to it across the ring) is equatorial. No hydrogen is anti to an equatorial Br. Z can react only through the flipped chair with tert-butyl axial, which about 1 molecule in 12,000 adopts: very slow.

[[chair:1d:Br,2u:CH3,4u:C(CH3)3|A]]

(b) X. Br is axial and the methyl, cis to Br, is equatorial. C2 has an axial H and so does C6. Both can leave, so the more substituted alkene forms: double bond between C1 and C2, toward the methyl (Saytzeff).

[[chair:1u:Br,2u:CH3,4u:C(CH3)3|A]]

Y. Br is axial and the methyl, trans to Br, is axial too. The H on C2 is equatorial and cannot leave. Only C6 has an axial H: double bond between C1 and C6, away from the methyl.

[[chair:1u:Br,2d:CH3,4u:C(CH3)3|A]]

rubric.h: Requirement stated, and tert-butyl equatorial fixes the chair
Z: Br equatorial in the locked chair, no anti H; reaction only through the rare chair with tert-butyl axial
X: Br axial, methyl equatorial, axial H on C2 and C6; Saytzeff alkene (C1=C2)
Y: Br axial, methyl axial, H on C2 equatorial; only C1=C6 can form

steps.h: tert-Butyl equatorial. A group on C1 that is cis to it (both up) is axial. A group on C1 that is trans to it is equatorial.

steps.t: Sort by the position of Br
steps.h: X and Y: Br up, cis to tert-butyl, axial. Z: Br down, equatorial. That alone explains fast, fast, slow.

steps.t: Place the methyl in X and Y
steps.h: With Br axial on C1, a methyl on C2 that is cis to Br is equatorial (X) and one that is trans is axial (Y).
X: C2 and C6. Y: C6 only. X gives the Saytzeff alkene, Y gives the alkene away from the methyl.

solution.answer: Z has Br locked equatorial: no anti H, very slow. X: axial H on C2 and C6, double bond toward the methyl. Y: methyl axial on C2, only C6 has an axial H, double bond away from the methyl.
solution.rule: tert-Butyl sets the chair, the leaving group's position sets the rate, the neighbours' axial hydrogens set the product.

stem:
Two bromocyclohexanes carry one deuterium (D) on the carbon next to the C-Br carbon. When the trans isomer undergoes {{E2}}, part of the product is cyclohexene that contains no deuterium. When the cis isomer reacts, every molecule of product still contains its deuterium. Explain what this shows about the {{E2}} reaction.

trans: [[ring:1u:Br,2d:D]] cis: [[ring:1u:Br,2u:D]]
model:
The result shows that {{E2}} removes only the atom that is anti-periplanar to the leaving group: on a cyclohexane, the axial atom on the next carbon, trans to an axial Br.

Trans isomer. In the chair with Br axial, D (trans to Br) is axial as well, and anti to Br. The base can remove D from C2, which gives cyclohexene with no deuterium. It can also remove the axial H from C6, which gives cyclohexene that keeps its D.

[[chair:1u:Br,2d:D|A]]

Cis isomer. In the chair with Br axial, D (cis to Br) is equatorial. The axial atom on C2 is H. The base removes that H, or the axial H on C6. D is never anti to Br, so it is never removed and every product molecule contains D.

[[chair:1u:Br,2u:D|A]]

If the base could take any neighbouring hydrogen regardless of geometry, both isomers would lose D part of the time. Only the isomer with D trans to Br loses it, so the elimination is anti.

rubric.h: Conclusion: E2 removes only the atom anti-periplanar (trans-diaxial) to the leaving group
Trans isomer: with Br axial, D is axial and anti, so it can be removed (D-free cyclohexene); H on C6 can also go
Cis isomer: with Br axial, D is equatorial; only H atoms are anti, so D always stays
Notes that loss of D from only one isomer rules out removal of a syn (cis) hydrogen

steps.t: Draw each chair with Br axial
steps.h: D behaves like H in size, so both chairs with Br axial are easy to reach. What matters is whether D ends up axial or equatorial.
Trans neighbours are both axial. D is anti to Br and can be the atom that leaves.
Cis neighbours are one axial, one equatorial. With Br axial, D is equatorial and the H on that carbon is the axial one.
The atom removed is always the one trans to the leaving group. This is direct evidence for anti elimination.

solution.answer: Only an atom anti (trans-diaxial) to Br is removed. D is axial and anti in the trans isomer, so it can be lost. In the cis isomer D is equatorial and is never lost.
solution.rule: E2 takes the hydrogen that is trans to the leaving group on the ring.
